scope: Standalone single-entry cacheable store admission and committed drain. No speculative holder, D-cache/refill, SQ/LSQ, forwarding, MMIO store path, shared data-port arbiter, production retirement wiring or full-core acceptance. No physical timing claim.
descriptor: Use a stable valid prepared SB/SH/SW descriptor. Full 13-bit ROB ID, address, size, word-relative mask and already shifted/masked 32-bit write data come from the preparation owner. Invalid/non-store/fault/uncached descriptors never qualify. Legal committed masks match size and natural alignment; unused write-data lanes are zero. fault_i must be checked even when uncached_i is zero because faulted preparation zeroes classification fields.
admission: admit_valid_i plus exact admit_id_i binds the current immutable descriptor to successful precommit admission. The future cache/target producer guarantees all required refill and permission checks have completed, resources/ownership remain reserved through commit, and admitted writes cannot report an architectural fault later. ROB ID alone is not permission to change descriptor bytes under an existing admission: any descriptor modification requires re-admission. This block does not establish that guarantee; no production producer exists yet. Production must never silently tie admission high.
retirement: commit_ready_o is eligibility, independent of commit_i. It requires empty capacity, valid nonfault cacheable store, exact live head ID and exact admission ID, and no reset/fatal/winning recovery/unsolicited response. commit_i is the final atomic retirement pulse, legal only when commit_ready_o is true. accept_o is their conjunction and must be the same edge as ROB/event/counter retirement and upstream descriptor consumption. One oldest-head store is admitted at a time; conservatively retire it alone in the future integration. No response-cycle refill or same-cycle turnover.
drain: Only accepted retirement captures ownership. The next cycle offers one cached masked-line write: aligned 32-byte address, prepared word bytes shifted into their line word, 32-bit byte mask, zero uncached fields. Offered valid and every request bit hold until acceptance, reset or fatal, independent of later descriptor, head, admission or recovery changes. A well-formed OK response releases ownership and advances the 4-bit bus ID. No cancellation input exists after capture.
ownership: busy_o, owner_id_o, line_address_o, line_mask_o and line_data_o expose the retained committed bytes through response completion, including while fatal is latched. Invalid views are zero. The future memory-order owner must block younger overlapping loads or forward these bytes, and fences/generation drain must wait for both this ownership and fatal handling. Until forwarding exists, conservatively block younger loads while busy. Neither request acceptance nor an untracked downstream queue may erase this ownership.
response: Only responses routed to this engine may be presented. The shared port has one outstanding transaction; future arbitration must record engine ownership rather than infer routing from the independently allocated 4-bit load/store IDs. Minimum response latency is one cycle. Responses must have the owned ID, OK or ACCESS_FAULT status, and zero read payload in both classes. The shared protocol architectural-fault effect applies to unretired accesses. Even an ACCESS_FAULT is fatal here because the store already retired and its admission guarantee was violated. A future MMIO store controller must instead retain architectural ownership until its response.
fatal: Registered sticky fatal_o latches the first fatal_reason_o: 0 none, 1 unexpected phase (unsolicited, early/same-request-cycle, or duplicate response), 2 wrong ID, 3 protocol/reserved status, 4 nonzero read payload, 5 postcommit access fault. Priority follows that list. Fatal suppresses commit/request/response channels, freezes held ownership and reason, and clears only on reset. There is no precise store-exception output. Global control must stop requests and retirement; busy alone is not a fatal indicator.
reset: Reset suppresses channels and ownership views, clears state/ID/fatal, and may lose an already retired but undrained store. This follows the platform reset contract, which also requires the target to suppress pre-reset responses. Recovery without reset never discards committed bytes. Fatal halts outstanding work rather than promising successful completion.
